title: India Ranks 100th of 122 in Global Hunger Index 2026, Wasting Near 19 Percent
excerpt: India's score improved to 24.1 and stunting fell to 29.3 percent, but the country stays in the 'serious' category with the highest child wasting rate in South Asia.
body:
• India ranked 100th of 122 countries in the Global Hunger Index 2026, released on October 14, with a score of 24.1 that keeps it in the 'serious' hunger category — up two places from 102nd of 123 in 2025.
  • Child wasting is the sharpest finding: 19.0 percent of children under five are wasted, the highest rate in South Asia, even as child stunting fell to 29.3 percent from 50.0 percent in 2000.
  • Undernourishment stands at 9.8 percent of the population and under-five mortality at 2.7 percent.
  • For families: the report points parents and caregivers to the programmes already in place — POSHAN 2.0 Anganwadi services, PM POSHAN school meals and the National Food Security Act's subsidised foodgrains — as the channels through which early-childhood nutrition support is delivered.

India has ranked 100th among 122 countries in the Global Hunger Index 2026, scoring 24.1 on the index's 100-point scale and remaining in the 'serious' hunger category. The report, titled "No Security Without Food Security," was released on October 14, 2026, ahead of World Food Day, and is published jointly by Concern Worldwide, Welthungerhilfe and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV). India shares the 100th rank with Ethiopia.

The four numbers behind the score

The index combines four indicators. For India, 9.8 percent of the population is undernourished. Child stunting — low height for age, a marker of chronic undernutrition — affects 29.3 percent of children under five. Child wasting — low weight for height, a marker of acute undernutrition — stands at 19.0 percent. Under-five mortality is 2.7 percent. A score between 20.0 and 34.9 falls in the serious category, and India's 24.1 sits in the middle of that band.

https://x.com/IndianGems_/status/2113235372545360100

The two child indicators are moving at different speeds. Stunting has fallen from 50.0 percent in 2000 to 29.3 percent, a drop of 20.7 percentage points, and has moved from the very high to the high category. Wasting has not followed it down. At 19.0 percent, India's child wasting rate is the highest in South Asia, according to the country summaries of the report published by Khan Global Studies. India's overall score has improved from 25.8 in 2018 to 24.1 in 2026, but the pace of improvement has slowed.

How India compares in South Asia

India trails three neighbours and leads two. Sri Lanka ranks 53rd with a score of 10.2, Nepal 72nd with 14.5, and Bangladesh 84th with 19.2 — all in the moderate category. Pakistan ranks 106th with 25.5 and Afghanistan 108th with 28.6, both serious. South Asia's regional score is 23.5 to 24.0 depending on the summary, against a global score of 18.1. Globally, hunger has worsened since 2018: the world score rose from 17.6 to 18.1, hunger levels increased in 32 countries, eight countries sit in the alarming category, and about 57 countries are projected to miss the low-hunger threshold by 2030 if current trends continue, The Orbit Post reported.

Context and the standing dispute

The report links hunger outcomes to more than food supply: access to diverse and affordable diets, maternal and child healthcare, sanitation and secure livelihoods all shape the indicators, and it flags climate extremes, food-price pressure and the prospect of below-normal monsoon rainfall across India's Monsoon Core Zone in 2026 as risks to food systems. India's existing response runs through Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, the PM POSHAN school-meals programme, subsidised foodgrains under the National Food Security Act of 2013, and the Anaemia Mukt Bharat campaign. The measurement itself is contested. In past years, the Indian government has rejected the index's methodology, arguing that stunting and child mortality reflect sanitation and health factors and not hunger alone, and citing its own Poshan Tracker data. The 2026 report does not settle that dispute.

What is next

The test the report sets is specific: whether wasting — the acute indicator, tied to recent illness, feeding in the first years of life and how quickly a child who is losing weight reaches treatment — can be brought down at anything like the pace stunting fell over two decades. The next editions of the index will show whether India's score moves faster than the slow improvement from 25.8 in 2018 to 24.1 in 2026. For now, India has gained two places in rank and remains, on this measure, a country with serious hunger and nearly three in ten young children stunted.
